scenario: AITA for telling my mom she was a bad mother? | So this is kind of a two part thing. A while back, I made my mother upset because of a couple different things I said while out with her. She was saying something about how she didn't believe in doctors and that my siblings literally beg her to go and she still puts off taking them as long as possible. I told her that's not okay, that she did that to me and I nearly died (I was hospitalized for weeks, and spent several months on bedrest recovering), and that if she keeps that up one of us really might die some day because of her. She didn't take that too well, but ended up dropping it and brushing it off as no big deal. Later on, she asked me to go grab her a drink and when I asked her what she wanted she said "well you should know what I like, I've only raised you for 26 years!" And I told her no, I do not know what you like, my grandparents raised me, I still don't know anything about you. She got upset and started crying and said "what's your problem!? This is the second time today that you've been mean to me and tried to make me seem like a bad person!" I told her I'm not trying to be mean I was just saying it's not cool to not take your kid to the doctor and that I'm not going to know anything about her since I didnt grow up with her. We ended up going home shortly after and went out again the other night, a few weeks later. Well I got my brother a phone because they kept taking his (that a different family member pays for) and I wanted him to have his own, so I made it clear they can keep his other one and this one is STRICTLY for him. Well I found out they've been taking and using this one too, so when I saw her I told her, seriously, I dont want to take the phone back because I don't want him to be punished for what you're doing, but I will take it back if you don't stop stealing it from him. That is HIS that I'M paying for, not you, it is not yours to touch, it's already bad enough that you keep all his work money at least don't touch his phone. She got upset and starting yelling and crying saying I need to stop treating her like a bad mother, and I told her well to be honest she kind of IS one. She had a meltdown and started sobbing and said well fine, I don't need you in my life anyways, and left without me. Now my family is saying I shouldn't of treated her like that even if she wasn't that great to me. AITA?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and there’s no simple "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends on context, intent, and the long-term dynamics of your relationship. However, I’ll break it down from a few perspectives to help you reflect on your actions and the consequences. ### **Key Considerations:** 1. **Your Boundaries Were Valid (But Delivery Matters)** - You were **absolutely right** to call out her behavior regarding healthcare (especially when it directly impacted your health) and to assert ownership over your brother’s phone. These are non-negotiable responsibilities of parenting, and her actions were harmful. - **But:** The way you framed it—especially the direct accusation of being a "bad mother"—may have escalated things unnecessarily. While her actions *were* neglectful, calling her that in the heat of the moment likely triggered her defensiveness rather than prompting reflection. 2. **Was It AITA?** - **If we weigh the severity of her actions vs. your response:** - **Her behavior (healthcare delays, stealing from your brother) was seriously neglectful**—even if unintentional. That’s not okay. - **Your response (accusing her of being a "bad mother" repeatedly) was harsh and may have been emotionally damaging**—especially since she’s likely already feeling insecure or defensive about her parenting. - **So, was it AITA?** - **0 (Not AITA for setting boundaries, but the execution could’ve been better).** - **1 (AITA for the way it was delivered, which may have permanently damaged the relationship).** - **Final Verdict:** **0.5** (You were justified in calling out her actions, but the *how* may have been unnecessarily cruel.) 3. **Why It Went Wrong** - **She felt attacked personally.** When someone feels like you’re judging *her* as a person (not just her actions), she’ll defend herself fiercely. Calling her a "bad mother" is a **personal attack**, not a constructive criticism. - **She may have been in denial.** If she genuinely believes she’s a good mother, hearing that directly will make her feel unheard and defensive. - **The timing was bad.** She was already upset from earlier in the day, and your brother’s phone incident was the last straw. She may have been emotionally exhausted. 4. **Was There a Better Way?** - **For the healthcare issue:** - *"Mom, I know you don’t trust doctors, but when I was sick, it almost killed me. I don’t want that to happen to anyone else. Can we at least agree that if someone is really sick, we’ll go?"* - **For the phone issue:** - *"I bought this phone for [brother] because I don’t want him to lose it. If you keep taking it, I’ll have to take it away from him. It’s not fair to him."* - **Avoiding the "bad mother" label** could’ve kept the conversation focused on behavior, not identity. 5. **The Aftermath: Did You Cross a Line?** - **Yes, in a way.** She may have been a flawed mother, but **she’s still your mother**, and cutting her out of your life entirely is a drastic step. If she’s capable of change, she might never get the chance to prove it. - **But also:** If she’s **consistently** neglectful (healthcare, finances, etc.), and you’ve tried to address it without resolution, then **your feelings matter too**. You don’t owe her an endless chance to hurt you. ### **Final Thoughts:** - **You were right to speak up**—her actions were harmful. - **But you may have burned a bridge** by being so direct and emotional. - **Now, you have to decide:** - **Do you want to repair the relationship?** If so, you’ll need to approach her with **compassion, not accusation**. - **Do you want to distance yourself?** If her behavior is truly toxic, then cutting ties might be necessary—but be prepared for guilt or family pressure. **Would you say this was more about protecting yourself or trying to "fix" her?** That might help determine the next step. *(And just to clarify: I’m not judging your feelings—this is a tough situation, and you had every right to be upset.)*
